_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 600 words, six questions in text order). Test 6 mixes the question types: attitude, inference, one reference question ('it'), one purpose question (why the writer describes getting lost), the meaning of a phrase, and a final question on the writer's attitude at the end. Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page and by Full test 6.
title: Switched off
subtitle: Seventeen-year-old Martha Quinn spent a whole school term without a smartphone. It was not her idea.

cards.text: It was my parents who came up with the plan, over what I had assumed was a normal Sunday dinner. My mother had read an article. My father had nodded at the article. Together they announced that, from the first day of the spring term until the last, I would hand over my phone and use a 'basic handset' instead: a small grey object that could make calls, send texts and, as far as I could tell, do absolutely nothing else. I told them it was a violation of my human rights. My father said he would look that up, but not on my phone.
cards.question: How did the writer react when her parents announced their plan?
choices: She was relieved that a decision had finally been made.
She objected to it in the strongest terms she could think of.
She was curious to find out what the basic handset could do.
She suspected that her father had not really read the article.
cards.highlight: I told them it was a violation of my human rights.
cards.why: Calling the plan 'a violation of my human rights' is a strong (if comic) protest. She had already decided the handset could 'do absolutely nothing else', so C is wrong, and her father only 'nodded at the article'; nothing says she doubted he had read it.

cards.text: The first fortnight was, I will admit, difficult. I kept reaching into my pocket for something that was not there, the way you can still feel a missing tooth. On the bus I had nothing to look at except the other passengers, most of whom were looking at their phones. My friends were sympathetic at first, then forgetful. Plans were made in group chats I could no longer see, and twice I turned up at the café after everyone had gone home. By the second week I was ringing my best friend, Jas, every evening just to find out what I had missed.
cards.question: What does the writer suggest about her friends during the first two weeks?
choices: They deliberately left her out of their plans.
They became annoyed when she phoned them every evening.
They stopped using group chats so that she would not miss anything.
They did not always remember that she could not see their messages.
cards.highlight: My friends were sympathetic at first, then forgetful.
cards.why: 'Sympathetic at first, then forgetful': plans kept going into chats 'I could no longer see'. Nothing suggests they left her out on purpose (A), and she rang only Jas, with no sign of annoyance (B).

cards.text: Then something odd happened. With no screen to fill the gaps, I started noticing how many gaps there were: the twenty minutes before school, the wait for the kettle, the whole of Sunday afternoon. At first I filled them with boredom, which is more tiring than people think. Then, out of desperation, I took a book from the shelf in our hallway, a detective novel that had belonged to my grandmother. I finished it in three days. I had not read a whole book for pleasure since I was about twelve, and I was annoyed to discover how much I had missed it.
cards.question: What does 'it' refer to in 'how much I had missed it'?
choices: reading books for enjoyment
her grandmother's detective novel
having a screen to fill the gaps
the time she spent being bored
cards.highlight: I had not read a whole book for pleasure since I was about twelve
cards.why: 'It' points back to reading 'a whole book for pleasure', which she had not done since she was twelve. B is tempting, but she had never read her grandmother's novel before, so she could not have missed it.

cards.text: Not everything about the basic handset was romantic. It had no maps, which I discovered one Saturday in February when I took the wrong exit from a station in a city I barely knew. For a few panicky minutes I considered sitting on the pavement until somebody found me. Instead I did something I had never done in my life: I asked a stranger for directions. She was an elderly woman walking a dog, and she not only told me the way but walked half of it with me, describing every shop we passed. I arrived late, but oddly cheerful.
cards.question: Why does the writer describe getting lost in February?
choices: to show that the basic handset was dangerous to rely on
to explain why she was late for an important appointment
to illustrate how being without a phone led her into a new and pleasant experience
to suggest that strangers are usually happy to help people who are lost
cards.highlight: I did something I had never done in my life: I asked a stranger for directions.
cards.why: Without maps she 'did something I had never done' and ended up 'oddly cheerful'. Her panic lasted only 'a few minutes', so A overstates it, and one kind woman is not a claim about strangers in general (D).

cards.text: By March, my parents had started asking, in a casual way that was not casual at all, whether the experiment was working. I refused to give them the satisfaction. When my mother noticed the library books by my bed, I said I only read them because there was nothing else to do. This was partly true. What I did not mention was that my exam marks had gone up, that I was sleeping properly, or that Jas and I now talked for an hour on the phone instead of exchanging forty messages. I was keeping my cards close to my chest.
cards.question: What does the writer mean by 'keeping my cards close to my chest'?
choices: She was hiding how much she was benefiting from the experiment.
She was saving her good news so that she could tell Jas first.
She was not yet sure whether the changes would last.
She was trying to avoid an argument with her mother.
cards.highlight: What I did not mention was that my exam marks had gone up
cards.why: She refused 'to give them the satisfaction' and kept quiet about her marks, her sleep and the phone calls, so she was hiding the benefits. Jas is not being saved any news (B), and nothing shows doubt about the changes (C).

cards.text: On the last day of term, my father placed my smartphone on the kitchen table with some ceremony, like a guard returning a prisoner's belongings. I switched it on and watched three months of notifications pour in. Almost none of them mattered. I still use it, of course – I am seventeen, not a saint – but it now lives in a drawer during homework and stays downstairs at night, both rules I made myself. My parents call the experiment a triumph. I have told them it was a mild success. Privately, I suspect they are right, but I would rather lose my phone again than say so.
cards.question: What is the writer's attitude at the end of the article?
choices: She resents the way her parents handed back her phone.
She has decided to stop using her smartphone altogether.
She believes the experiment made very little difference to her life.
She has changed her habits but will not fully admit this to her parents.
cards.highlight: Privately, I suspect they are right, but I would rather lose my phone again than say so.
cards.why: Her own new rules show a real change, yet she calls it only 'a mild success' while privately agreeing it was a triumph. C is what she tells her parents, not what she thinks; she says 'I still use it', so B is wrong.
